In Syria, delivering sensitive news bluntly is not the usual expectation. People there generally prefer a softer approach when giving feedback or information that could be disappointing. In Canada, the idea that younger people typically enter a room first is not the usual expectation. In Poland, skipping or rushing the greeting is not acceptable; it is seen as rude. The businessperson should therefore take the time to greet the colleague properly before moving on to business. In Chile, businesswomen are commonly addressed by their first name in professional settings. This reflects a preference for a more informal and direct style of communication in business interactions. In Croatia, using the left hand alone to offer or receive something is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use the right hand or both hands when giving or taking an item. In Israel, pointing with the index finger is not the usual way to indicate direction. In New Zealand, the left hand is not the usual choice for passing or receiving items. The common expectation is to use the right hand for such exchanges. In Mexico, the idea that the couple themselves generally pay for the wedding expenses is not the usual expectation. In Somalia, dropping by someone's home without prior arrangement is not the usual expectation. In Germany, sexually suggestive jokes are not generally seen as appropriate in a workplace break conversation. In Ukraine, a direct 'no' is not usually seen as clear, honest, and respectful; it can come across as abrupt or even rude. In France, shaking hands with the left hand is not the usual practice. The common expectation is to use the right hand when greeting someone. In North Macedonia, a neutral expression when meeting someone new is not the usual expectation. People there generally smile when they meet a new colleague for the first time. In Afghanistan, the elderly are not treated as ordinary passengers; they are given special respect. In Cambodia, a gentle handshake with averted eyes is not the usual way colleagues greet each other at a business meeting. The common expectation is a firm handshake accompanied by direct eye contact. In Taiwan, praise is not usually reserved for exceptional achievements. In Malta, a quick lifting of the eyebrows is commonly understood as a nonverbal way of saying “no.” This gesture is used in response to a question, and it serves as a brief, non-verbal refusal. In Ireland, a brief nod is not the usual way acquaintances greet each other on the street. The common expectation is a verbal greeting, typically 'hi' or 'hello', accompanied by a handshake. In Laos, the idea that peers are approached first during greetings is not the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption toward others is important, so greetings are ordered by age. In Sudan, gift wrapping and cards are not a common practice for birthday presents. The expectation is that gifts are presented without wrapping or a card. In Croatia, white is not typically associated with purity and is not a common choice for festive occasions like weddings. In North Macedonia, standing while others are seated is not the usual expectation. This shows consideration for the group and fits the common practice of joining others at the same level.

In Hungary, the idea that women generally maintain direct eye contact with men is not the usual expectation. In Afghanistan, pointing with the index finger is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as rude. The visitor should avoid using the index finger to gesture to the server. In Sri Lanka, the expectation that a newly married couple must live with the husband's parents is not the usual practice. In Fiji, close friends do not typically greet each other with a handshake. The common expectation among close friends is to hug and kiss each other on the cheek. In Myanmar, entering a room without knocking when the door is closed is not the usual expectation. Avoiding disruption or offense to others matters, so people generally knock before entering a closed room. The colleague should knock on the door before entering. This shows consideration for whoever is inside and respects their privacy. Simply opening the door without knocking could be seen as intrusive or disrespectful.

In Syria, people generally value avoiding offense or disruption in their interactions with others. In Germany, close friends and family do not usually keep their distance during conversations. It is common for them to touch each other often, such as by patting a hand or arm, while talking. This kind of physical contact is a normal part of friendly interaction between people who are close.

In Austria, a direct apology by saying "I am sorry" is not the usual way to handle a minor accident like stepping on someone's foot. In Mauritius, pointing directly at a person is not the usual way to indicate someone. The common expectation is to avoid pointing at a person directly. Instead, the visitor should gesture toward the person without pointing. This approach is more appropriate in this situation.

In Chile, keeping shoes on when entering a mosque is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to remove shoes before stepping inside a place of worship. In Ireland, receiving a business card with the left hand only is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to accept the card with both hands or with the right hand only. This shows respect and attentiveness in a professional setting. Using the left hand alone can be seen as careless or disrespectful. In the United States, it is not unusual for an older relative to ask a young adult whether they are married yet. This question is a common expectation at family gatherings, especially when the young adult is of marriageable age. The older relative would most likely ask whether the young adult is married yet. In Greece, a guest is not expected to decline what the host offers, especially chai. The common expectation is to accept the offer, as it is a gesture of hospitality and goodwill. In North Macedonia, the idea that women are expected to use casual and direct styles of communication that imply equality is not accurate. In Croatia, receiving a gift with one hand is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to accept a gift with both hands, as this shows respect and appreciation for the gesture. In Chile, it is not the usual expectation to wait for the host or server to refill a colleague's teacup. The common practice is to offer to refill the cup yourself. In Chile, counting change in front of a cashier is not the usual expectation. People there generally try to avoid actions that might cause offense or discomfort to others. In Mauritius, a direct and blunt response is not the usual way to handle a question about a project timeline. In Palestine, arriving late to a scheduled meeting is not the usual expectation. Punctuality is generally valued, and people are expected to arrive on time for appointments. In Zimbabwe, answering or using a mobile phone during a business meeting is not the usual expectation. In Kenya, there is a common belief that breaking a mirror brings bad luck. To prevent this misfortune, people often knock on wood three times. In Bangladesh, arranging a meeting at short notice is not the usual expectation. In Cyprus, the idea that men are not expected to open doors for women is not accurate. In the United States, it is common for women to act warm and engaged on a first date with someone they like. In Ireland, the idea that elders are not necessarily to be respected does not reflect the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption toward others is important, and this includes showing consideration to older people. On a crowded bus, a young adult is generally expected to offer their seat to an elderly passenger who boards and stands nearby. In Canada, remaining seated when greeting someone is not the usual expectation. When a visitor enters the office, the employee is generally expected to stand up. In Afghanistan, taking more food than one can eat is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as wasteful and disrespectful to the host. Taking a large portion that might go uneaten would go against this expectation of care and consideration.

In Afghanistan, older women do not typically socialise in public places like cafes or parks. The common expectation is that they meet in private settings, such as at home. For this social visit, the two older women would most likely meet at one of their homes. In Syria, entering a shop without greeting anyone is not the usual expectation. People there generally expect a customer to acknowledge the staff when they come in. In rural Colombia, it is not the case that people remain silent when passing others. On a path in a rural area, it is common to greet the other person with a simple 'buenos días' or 'buenas tardes' depending on the time of day. This is a friendly acknowledgment of the other person's presence. Therefore, the person should greet the other person with a simple 'buenos días' or 'buenas tardes'. Remaining silent would feel cold or unfriendly in this setting.

In South Sudan, sitting with legs spread apart and slouched is not the usual expectation at a formal dinner. The common practice is to sit upright with legs together and feet on the floor. This posture is seen as appropriate for a formal setting, showing respect for the occasion and the hosts. Therefore, the person should sit upright with legs together and feet on the floor. In Samoa, a coffee break conversation between colleagues is not expected to stay serious and on the topic at hand. In South Sudan, giving sharp objects like knives or scissors as a housewarming gift is not the usual expectation. In Palestine, a meeting does not typically begin directly with business matters without personal small talk. In Indonesia, public displays of emotion, affection, or attachment are not uncommon and are generally accepted. This behavior is seen as a normal expression of feelings in a public setting. Therefore, the couple would likely embrace and kiss each other before parting, rather than keeping their distance.

In South Sudan, avoiding eye contact when greeting someone is not the usual practice. People there generally make eye contact while greeting a new colleague. In Portugal, openly celebrating and taking pride in a promotion is not the usual expectation. Humility is valued, and people are expected to limit self-importance and avoid status display. In Ireland, the left hand is not the usual choice for passing or receiving items. The common expectation is to use the right hand for such exchanges. In Singapore, direct eye contact is not expected to be held continuously without diverting the gaze. A common expectation is to maintain eye contact for a while, then look away occasionally. This pattern is seen as a natural part of conversation rather than a sign of discomfort or lack of attention. Therefore, the person should maintain eye contact for a while, then look away occasionally. Doing so fits the local conversational style and helps the interaction feel comfortable and respectful.

In Austria, visiting a friend is not typically done before a meal or on weekdays. The common expectation is to visit someone in the late afternoon or on Sundays. This timing allows for a relaxed visit without interrupting meal preparations or weekday routines. Therefore, the person should visit the friend in the late afternoon or on Sunday. Visiting before a meal or on a weekday would not fit this preference.

In Sweden, swearing in front of a woman is not the usual expectation. Many men there try to avoid using offensive language when a woman is present. This fits the situation because it shows consideration for his female colleague without disrupting the interaction. In Japan, the idea that people are expected to be reserved toward strangers does not reflect the usual practice. When a traveler arrives at a family's home in the evening after a long journey, the family is generally expected to be welcoming and hospitable. This means offering the traveler a place to stay, food, and a warm welcome. The family should therefore invite the traveler to stay, offer food, and give a warm welcome. In Pakistan, close friends and family commonly greet each other with a handshake or a brief hug. In South Korea, a visitor is not expected to arrive without prior notice, as spontaneous visits are not welcome. In Brazil, an elderly neighbor would not typically greet a young adult using the person's formal given name. The common expectation is that older people use the first name when greeting others. In Somalia, leaving the shoulders uncovered when visiting a church is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to cover the shoulders as a sign of respect for the sacred space. In Zimbabwe, arriving late without prior notice is not acceptable, even if the delay is short. In Iraq, it is not uncommon for couples to display affection in public. On a sunny afternoon in a park, a couple would typically hold hands or walk close together. This kind of physical closeness is a normal expression of their relationship in that setting. Keeping a noticeable distance would be less typical and might seem distant or formal. Therefore, the customary thing for the couple to do is to hold hands or walk close together.

In Chile, the idea that people generally avoid asking friends for personal favours and support is not accurate. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, a handshake between colleagues in the office hallway is not usually firm and accompanied by averted gaze. In South Sudan, a guest is not expected to greet only the host upon entering a gathering. The common expectation is to greet everyone present, including the host and all other acquaintances. In Ireland, the idea that newlyweds usually move into a home of their own after marriage is not the common expectation. In North Macedonia, tipping is a routine and expected part of dining out. It is common to leave a tip of around 10% of the bill, especially for good service. In Malaysia, a verbal greeting without physical contact is not the usual way for men to greet each other in a business setting. Therefore, in this situation, the two men should shake hands. A verbal greeting alone would feel incomplete and less warm than a handshake would.

In Ukraine, addressing a colleague by only their first name without any title is not the usual practice when meeting for the first time. In Portugal, directly pointing out a colleague's mistake during a team presentation is not the usual way to handle such a situation. In Russia, the idea that families live independently from their extended family is not the usual expectation. It is common for three generations to live together in the same household. In Taiwan, suggesting a meeting is not a casual gesture that can be left hanging.
